silicon-photonics-001.question: Which value is closest to the relative index difference Δ = (n₁² − n₂²)/(2n₁²) of a waveguide with a silicon core (refractive index 3.48) surrounded by oxide (refractive index 1.44)?
silicon-photonics-001.explanation: Δ = (3.48² − 1.44²) / (2 × 3.48²) = (12.11 − 2.07) / 24.2 ≈ 0.41, or about 41%. About 0.4% is the value for standard single-mode fiber (Δ ≈ 0.3–0.4%); silicon waveguides have about 100 times that index contrast. About 83% drops the 2 in the denominator. A large index contrast confines light strongly, allowing bend radii down to a few micrometers and cross sections of a few hundred nanometers, so devices can be integrated densely. The price is larger scattering loss from sidewall roughness and larger changes in characteristics from slight dimensional variations.

silicon-photonics-002.question: On 220 nm thick SOI, which width is closest to that of a standard silicon wire waveguide that guides TE-polarized light in the 1550 nm band as single-mode?
silicon-photonics-002.explanation: In high-contrast silicon wire waveguides, the width is typically about 450–500 nm for a 220 nm thickness, so that higher-order modes are not guided. A wider waveguide also guides higher-order TE modes, while one that is too narrow lets light spread far into the oxide, increasing sidewall scattering and leakage into the substrate. About 8–10 µm is the core size of a low-contrast optical fiber; a silicon waveguide that wide would carry many modes. At about 50 nm, light can hardly be confined at all. Waveguide dimensions of a fraction of the wavelength are the source of silicon photonics' compactness.

silicon-photonics-003.question: Which correctly describes the relation between the effective index n_eff and the group index n_g of a silicon wire waveguide? (λ is the vacuum wavelength.)
choices: n_g and n_eff are always equal
n_g = n_eff − λ dn_eff/dλ, and in silicon wires n_g is larger than n_eff (for example n_g ≈ 4.2 for n_eff ≈ 2.4)
n_g = n_eff + λ dn_eff/dλ, and n_g is always smaller than n_eff
silicon-photonics-003.explanation: The effective index describes the phase velocity of the guided mode, and the group index describes the group velocity (energy velocity) at which pulses and envelopes travel; they are related by n_g = n_eff − λ dn_eff/dλ. In silicon wires, light spreads further into the oxide at longer wavelengths, lowering n_eff (dn_eff/dλ < 0), so the group index is larger than the effective index, around 4. The two are equal only in a dispersionless medium. The formula with the opposite sign is wrong. A key design point is that the ring-resonator FSR, the wavelength period of a Mach–Zehnder interferometer and the delay of a delay line all use the group index.

silicon-photonics-004.question: Which value is closest to the free spectral range (FSR) near 1550 nm of a silicon ring resonator with a radius of 10 µm (group index 4.2, effective index 2.4)? (FSR = λ²/(n_g L), where L is the circumference.)
silicon-photonics-004.explanation: The circumference is L = 2π × 10 µm ≈ 62.8 µm, so FSR = λ²/(n_gL) = (1.55×10⁻⁶)² / (4.2 × 62.8×10⁻⁶) ≈ 9.1×10⁻⁹ m, or about 9.1 nm. About 16 nm uses the effective index of 2.4 instead of the group index, a large difference in highly dispersive silicon wires. About 57 nm uses the radius instead of the circumference. Because the FSR sets the usable wavelength range of a wavelength-multiplexed circuit, rings are made smaller to widen the FSR when many channels are needed. A smaller radius, however, increases bending loss and lowers Q, so the size is chosen as a compromise.

silicon-photonics-005.question: Which value is closest to the Q (loaded Q) of a ring resonator whose resonance in the transmission spectrum has a full width at half maximum of 0.05 nm at 1550 nm?
silicon-photonics-005.explanation: Q is the resonance wavelength divided by the full width at half maximum: Q = λ/Δλ = 1550 / 0.05 = 3.1×10⁴. About 3.2×10⁻⁵ is the reciprocal. About 1.6×10⁴ is off by a factor of 2, as if the linewidth were taken as 0.1 nm. Q also corresponds to the time light stays in the resonator (photon lifetime τ = Q/ω = Qλ/(2πc)), here about 25 ps. Higher Q gives sharper filters and modulators that work at lower power, but the photon lifetime limits modulation bandwidth, and the tolerance to resonance shifts from temperature and fabrication variation becomes narrower.

silicon-photonics-006.question: For a ring resonator coupled to a bus waveguide, in which coupling regime does the through-port transmission at the resonance wavelength fall nearly to zero?
choices: Overcoupling (coupling much larger than the round-trip loss)
Undercoupling (coupling much smaller than the round-trip loss)
Critical coupling (coupling between ring and bus equal to the loss over one round trip of the ring)
silicon-photonics-006.explanation: The through-port output is set by the interference between light that passes straight by without entering the ring and light that circulates in the ring and comes back out. At critical coupling, where the coupling equals the round-trip loss, the two have equal amplitude and opposite phase at resonance, so they cancel completely and the transmission is zero. All the light that enters the ring is lost inside it. With overcoupling the returning light is too strong, and with undercoupling too weak, so cancellation is incomplete and some transmission remains. Overcoupling broadens the resonance linewidth, suiting fast modulators and wide-passband filters. Ring modulators that need maximum extinction ratio are designed near critical coupling.

silicon-photonics-007.question: Take the temperature coefficient of the effective index of a silicon waveguide as about 1.8×10⁻⁴ /K and the group index as 4.2. Which value is closest to the temperature-induced shift of the resonance wavelength of a 1550 nm ring resonator (Δλ/ΔT = λ (dn_eff/dT) / n_g)?
silicon-photonics-007.explanation: Δλ/ΔT = 1550 nm × 1.8×10⁻⁴ / 4.2 ≈ 0.066 nm/K, or about 0.07 nm/K. About 0.28 nm/K forgets to divide by the group index, and about 0.12 nm/K divides by the effective index (about 2.4) instead. A temperature change of only 10 K shifts the resonance by about 0.7 nm, far more than the linewidth (tens of picometers) of a ring with a Q in the tens of thousands. That is why heaters and feedback temperature control are almost essential for silicon rings. Conversely, this large thermo-optic effect lets a filter's wavelength be tuned with little power.

silicon-photonics-008.question: In a thermo-optic phase shifter that heats a 100 µm long silicon waveguide, which value is closest to the temperature rise needed to shift the phase of 1.55 µm light by π? (Temperature coefficient of the index 1.8×10⁻⁴ /K; assume the light is fully confined in the waveguide.)
silicon-photonics-008.explanation: The phase change is Δφ = (2π/λ) × (dn/dT) × ΔT × L. Setting Δφ = π gives ΔT = λ / (2L × dn/dT) = 1.55×10⁻⁶ / (2 × 100×10⁻⁶ × 1.8×10⁻⁴) ≈ 43 K. About 86 K is the temperature needed for a 2π phase change (one full wavelength), and about 4.3 K is the value for a 1 mm length, an order-of-magnitude error. A longer phase shifter needs a smaller temperature rise, but the heated volume grows, so the power consumption (Pπ, typically a few tens of milliwatts) does not fall much. Etching away the oxide and substrate around the waveguide to keep heat from escaping can greatly reduce Pπ.

silicon-photonics-009.question: In a directional coupler formed by bringing two waveguides close together, let Lc be the length at which light launched into one waveguide transfers completely to the other (the full coupling length). What coupling length splits the light equally between the two outputs (a 3 dB coupler)? (Assume the two waveguides are identical and phase-matched.)
silicon-photonics-009.explanation: In a phase-matched directional coupler, the fraction of power transferred to the other waveguide varies as sin²(κL) (κ is the coupling coefficient), with complete transfer at κLc = π/2. An equal split needs sin²(κL) = 1/2, that is, κL = π/4, so L = Lc/2. At Lc/4, only sin²(π/8) ≈ 15% transfers. At Lc, all the light moves to the other waveguide. Directional couplers are simple and low-loss, but because the coupling coefficient is sensitive to waveguide gap and wavelength, the split ratio drifts easily with fabrication variation and is hard to keep constant over a wide wavelength range.

silicon-photonics-010.question: Why are multimode interference (MMI) couplers often used for splitting light in silicon photonics?
choices: Because they are narrow waveguides that carry only a single mode, so they have no loss at all
Because they automatically align the polarization of light
Because they use self-imaging from the interference of many modes in a wide waveguide, so the split ratio tends to stay stable against dimensional variation and wavelength changes
silicon-photonics-010.explanation: An MMI coupler launches light into a wide waveguide (the multimode region) and uses the self-imaging effect, in which interference among many modes periodically reproduces the input image. Placing output waveguides where the image splits in two at the right length gives a 1×2 or 2×2 splitter. MMIs tolerate dimensional errors well and depend less on wavelength than directional couplers, so they are widely used for the splitting and combining sections of Mach–Zehnder modulators. As the name says, an MMI uses a multimode region; its excess loss is small but not zero. It does not align polarization either, and the self-imaging length differs for TE and TM.

silicon-photonics-011.question: When a silicon Mach–Zehnder modulator (MZM) is used to transmit intensity-modulated digital signals (NRZ) or PAM4, which operating point is generally set with the DC bias?
choices: The point of maximum transmission (zero phase difference)
The quadrature point, where transmission is about half its maximum (a π/2 phase difference between the arms)
The point of minimum transmission (a phase difference of π)
silicon-photonics-011.explanation: The transmission of an MZM varies as cos²(Δφ/2) with the phase difference Δφ between its two arms. At the quadrature point, with a π/2 phase difference, the transmission is half its maximum and the curve is steepest and closest to linear, so the intensity changes in proportion to the electrical signal amplitude, and distortion stays low even for multilevel amplitudes such as PAM4. At the points of maximum or minimum transmission, the slope of the curve is zero, so small signals barely change the intensity and the modulation frequency is doubled. Note that in IQ modulators for coherent communications, which modulate phase and amplitude, each MZM is biased at minimum transmission to flip the sign of the field.

silicon-photonics-012.question: A silicon modulator has a VπL (the product of the voltage needed for a π phase shift and the phase-shifter length) of 2 V·cm, and its phase shifter is 3 mm long. Which value is closest to Vπ?
silicon-photonics-012.explanation: Vπ = VπL / L = 2 V·cm / 0.3 cm ≈ 6.7 V. About 0.67 V is the unit error of taking the length as 3 cm, and about 67 V takes it as 0.03 cm. Because the free-carrier dispersion effect in silicon is weak, Vπ is several volts, and with the output swing of CMOS drivers (around 1 V) the phase swing is small and the modulation depth tends to be insufficient. A longer phase shifter lowers Vπ, but long electrodes reduce bandwidth through RF loss and velocity mismatch with the light, and optical loss increases too. Approaches include push-pull drive, traveling-wave electrodes, ring modulators, or combining other materials such as thin-film lithium niobate.

silicon-photonics-013.question: You want a silicon grating coupler to couple 1.55 µm light from air at 10° from the normal. If the effective index of the light guided by the grating is 2.8, which value is closest to the required grating period? (Phase-matching condition Λ = λ/(n_eff − sinθ).)
silicon-photonics-013.explanation: The phase-matching condition says that the wavenumber set by the grating period makes up the difference between the wavenumbers of the guided light and the obliquely incident light. Λ = 1.55 / (2.8 − sin10°) = 1.55 / (2.8 − 0.174) ≈ 0.590 µm, or about 590 nm. About 554 nm ignores the sinθ term as if the angle were 0°, and about 521 nm reverses the sign of sinθ. Coupling is not done from directly above (θ = 0°) because under that condition Bragg reflection back into the waveguide becomes strong and efficiency falls, so a tilt of about 8–10° is typical. Because the period determines the wavelength that couples, grating couplers are limited to a bandwidth of a few tens of nanometers.

silicon-photonics-014.question: When intense light at 1.55 µm (several hundred milliwatts or more) is launched into a silicon waveguide, the loss increases with intensity. What is the main cause?
choices: Two-photon absorption (TPA) and the free-carrier absorption caused by the carriers it generates
The energy of a single 1.55 µm photon exceeds the band gap of silicon, so it is absorbed by single photons
The silicon crystal melts under intense light and becomes amorphous
silicon-photonics-014.explanation: The energy of a 1.55 µm photon (about 0.8 eV) is below the band gap of silicon (about 1.12 eV), so single photons are not absorbed. Two together, however, give 1.6 eV and exceed the gap, so in narrow waveguides with high intensity, two-photon absorption — the simultaneous absorption of two photons — occurs. Its probability is proportional to the square of intensity, and the electrons and holes it creates add free-carrier absorption, increasing loss further. Sweeping the carriers out with a reverse-biased pin junction suppresses part of this. Because of this effect, silicon has limits for nonlinear optics and high-power transmission, and silicon nitride, which has no two-photon absorption, is sometimes used. Melting does not occur at ordinary continuous-wave intensities.

silicon-photonics-015.question: Which correctly describes a modulator based on a ring resonator (ring modulator) compared with a Mach–Zehnder modulator (MZM)?
choices: It is large and consumes more power, but its characteristics do not change with temperature at all
It has the same characteristics over a wide wavelength range, so no wavelength tuning is needed
It is small with low capacitance, so it runs at low power, but its resonance wavelength shifts easily with temperature and fabrication variation, so wavelength tuning is needed
silicon-photonics-015.explanation: A ring modulator is small, a few to a dozen or so micrometers across, and resonance enhances the phase change, so a short phase shifter produces a large change in intensity. Its low capacitance keeps drive power low, and several rings with different resonance wavelengths can be lined up along one bus waveguide to build a compact wavelength-multiplexed transmitter. On the other hand, operating on resonance means a narrow usable wavelength range, and a 1 K temperature change shifts the resonance by about 0.07 nm, so heater tuning and control are essential. There is also a bandwidth limit from the photon lifetime and chirp accompanying the intensity change. An MZM is long and large but works over a wide wavelength range and is relatively robust to temperature changes.
